title: Letters close
hookLine: sixty letters read of one hundred and twenty-four

cards: The letters open the same way. In Latin: Seneca Lucilio suo salutem. Seneca greets his Lucilius.
Not Lucilius. His Lucilius. And they close with a single word: vale.
Be well. Farewell. About two months ago we opened the first one, an old man in Italy writing to a friend in Sicily about how to hold an hour.
Of the one hundred and twenty-four letters that survive, we've read from sixty. Tomorrow Seneca's essays begin. Today we fold the stack.

teach.h: SIXTY LETTERS, SHORT LINES TO CARRY.
teach.b: First, what was in the stack. Hold every hour. Who is poor.
Choose, then trust. All mine is with me, said Stilpo, who'd lost everything. They're people, not just slaves.
Harpaste, where the blindness is ours. Ictus animi and its first jolt. Apes.
Cleanthes. Ratio. Sixty letters, and each left a line short enough to carry.

teach.h: A DAILY PAYMENT, OFTEN FROM EPICURUS.
teach.b: In the early letters, Seneca keeps ending with a saying he's found, often from Epicurus, a rival school. He calls it his daily payment to Lucilius.
A teacher who takes good lines from wherever they grow: that's this whole path's method too. Third, the missing half.
We have none of Lucilius' replies. Not one. Seneca answers questions we never hear asked.
Scholars even debate whether this was a real exchange, a book written in the shape of letters, or some of each. We're left reading one side of a phone call. Fourth, why that's a gift.
The empty half is where the reader sits.
For sixty days, you've been Lucilius: the friend being written to, scolded, encouraged, sent a line at the bottom of the page. Every letter ended with vale, and waited. Tonight you get to answer.

how: Some readers finish Seneca's letters by writing a letter back to him, naming what helped, what they tried and where they disagree.

games.q: you've read sixty letters addressed to someone else's friend. Seneca ends each one: vale. what's left to do?
o: read all sixty again at once.
games.why: Lucilius' half is missing; the path asks you to fill it with a letter of your own.

practice: Start a letter in your head, or on paper if you have it: Dear Seneca, then one line of his that helped, one thing you tried because of him, and one place you'd push back, on the wealth, the court, the harsh consolation.
Be honest; he was. If you like, end the way he always did: vale, be well.

wordCard.voice: Vale. The word that closes every one of Seneca's letters: be well, farewell, after sixty read of the one hundred twenty-four that survive. Today's word.
